breaks.quote: So ask it straight. And when you cannot answer, tell it as a story about somebody else and find the moral.
breaks.why: The ask is a specific action, but it rests on the chimpanzee story and is squeezed into two sentences, so a doubtful reader can shrug.

breaks.quote: Because it is not finished with you. It still has a lesson to teach, and you have not learned it yet.
breaks.why: The key reason that regret carries a lesson is only stated, not argued or shown in the reader's life, so the reader must take it on trust.

breaks.quote: If the answer is no, prune. Pick something that still matters to you and prune it.
breaks.why: The ask to end things that still matter rests mainly on the writer's own story, with the reader's own case given only in a short list, so a doubtful reader can shrug.

breaks.quote: Pruning hurts, and it will hurt you too.
breaks.why: The cost is named in one sentence and answered only by saying they can restart later, which does not meet the reader's doubt about losing something that matters.

breaks.quote: Don't wait for it to become useless first, because you may never be able to call any of them useless.
breaks.why: The ask is squeezed into the last paragraphs, and the reason why this change beats an easier one is a single sentence.
